summary: Introduces the STD subseries of notes within the RFC series. STDs identify clearly which RFCs document Internet standards, so people can tell standards from other documents.

plainLanguage.summary: Most RFCs are just notes. This paper introduces a special shelf, called STD, that holds only the ones that are official standards.

subtitle: How the STD subseries labels which RFCs document Internet standards, and how STD numbers work.

tldr.problem: Readers could not easily tell which RFCs documented Internet standards and which were other kinds of notes.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB creates the STD subseries. A specification that reaches the Standard maturity level gets an STD number, which stays the same even when the document is replaced by a new RFC.
tldr.outcome: An STD number identifies a standard, while an RFC number identifies a document. The memo is Informational and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 1311 is an Informational memo and, according to its metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. Its list of STD numbers is the grandfathered set as of March 1992.

sections.title: What the STD Subseries Is
sections.content: The STDs are a subseries of notes within the RFC series that are the Internet standards. The intent is to identify clearly for the Internet community which RFCs document Internet standards. They stay in the RFC series because its distribution and maintenance mechanisms are already in place, and anyone who can get an RFC can get an STD.
sections.plainLanguage: STD is a label for the RFCs that are official rules. It lets people find the real rules quickly among all the other notes.

sections.title: How STD Numbers Work
sections.content:
An STD number is assigned when a specification reaches the Standard maturity level and the IAB has designated it a standard. Both Technical Specifications and Applicability Statements qualify. The standard for a particular protocol always keeps the same STD number.

An STD number identifies a standard, not a document. If a standard is spread over several documents, they each carry the same number. The Domain Name System is specified by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, both labelled STD-13, so the full citation is "STD-13/RFC-1034/RFC-1035". If a standard is reworked into a new document, the new RFC gets a new RFC number but the same STD number, and no version numbers are attached to STD numbers.

Separate STD numbers are used when specifications are logically separable, as with the Telnet Options. Amendments and non-optional extensions reuse the base number. The memo's summary is that an acronym like TCP refers to a concept, an RFC number like RFC-793 indicates a specific version of the specification, and an STD number like STD-7 designates the status.
sections.plainLanguage: An STD number is like a jersey number for a position on a team. The player can change, but the number stays, and each new document keeps the old number.

sections.title: Format Rules and Publication
sections.content:
STD RFCs follow the format rules of RFC 1111. Each must have a "Status of this Memo" section on the first page that conveys the status approved by the IAB, a distribution statement (normally "Distribution of this memo is unlimited."), a Security Considerations section, and an author's address at the very end with name, postal address, telephone number and email address.

New documents can become STD RFCs only through an action of the IAB, and the RFC Editor publishes them. They are announced and obtained the same way as any RFC. The current standards are listed in the "IAB Official Protocol Standards", which is STD-1, with RFC 1280 as its current edition.
sections.plainLanguage: Each official paper must follow the same checklist: a label saying what it is, a note about who may share it, a safety section and the author's address.

sections.title: The Grandfathered STDs
sections.content: The appendix assigns STD numbers to the existing standards. Examples are STD 5 for IP, ICMP and IGMP, STD 6 for UDP, STD 7 for TCP, STD 9 for FTP and STD 13 for the Domain Name System. STDs 27 to 32 cover Telnet options. Some entries combine several RFCs under one STD, such as STDs 5, 13 and 20.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix is the first list of the shelf. The older official rules were given their numbers all at once.
